edge.title: The fare argument you can lose and still win
edge.setup: The meter and the driver's demand differ, you are tired, and the driver is getting louder. You are right, it is your money, and every instinct says to stand your ground at the roadside.
edge.tell: If a dispute is about a few hundred rupees and the other person is angry, being right is not worth staying in range.
move: Step out and put distance between you and the vehicle before you argue further; pay what you consider fair or walk away, whichever ends the contact sooner.
Photograph the number plate and note the time and place, so you can complain afterwards from a safe spot.
Report it to the Bengaluru traffic police or the app's support afterwards; the complaint works the same an hour later, and you will be there to file it.
edge.why: Fare fights escalate because both sides feel the principle matters more than the amount. The amount is small and recoverable, while a confrontation with an angry person is not. Ending physical contact first and complaining later keeps the principle and removes the risk.
edge.variants: Same shape: parking disputes, road rage after a minor scrape, delivery or cab-cancellation arguments, a noisy neighbour at your door.

scenario.question: An auto driver demands ₹150 more than the meter and starts shouting as you step out. What do you do?

choices.text: Move away, note the plate number, and complain to the traffic police later.
Stay and argue until he accepts the meter fare; it is a matter of principle.
Pay the extra ₹150 with no record and leave without noting anything.

edge.anchor: An auto driver was arrested for killing an advocate over a fare dispute in Bengaluru (The Times of India).

lens.name: Chesterton's fence
lens.one_line: Before removing something that looks pointless, find out why it was put there.
lens.detail: A rule, a process or a fence in a field that serves no visible purpose may be solving a problem you can't see precisely because it's being solved. The discipline isn't conservatism — it's the requirement to understand the original reason first, after which you may well still remove it, but now knowing the cost.
elsewhere: A weird approval step that quietly prevents a rare, expensive error.
Legacy code nobody dares delete, for reasons occasionally excellent.
A family practice that looks superstitious and encodes something practical.
lens.test: Do I understand why this exists? If not, I'm not yet qualified to remove it.
lens.today: North Bengaluru areas have been battling power cuts for three months after Metro work damaged a Bescom cable (The Times of India). Digging for a new line is easy to justify; the cable already in the ground was solving a problem nobody at the surface was tracking. Before you cheer or curse a civic project, ask what the old thing was quietly doing.

moved.what: Bengaluru leads post-SIR voter activity, with Form 6 applications up 32% (The Times of India).
moved.so_what: If you moved or turned 18 recently, check your name on the electoral roll now rather than at the next election.

moved.what: Retired railway employees across Bengaluru, Hubballi and Mysuru divisions can now submit life certificates online (The Times of India).
moved.so_what: If a parent draws a railway pension, the online route saves a queue; set it up for them before their certificate is due.

moved.what: North Bengaluru areas are facing power cuts for three months after Metro work damaged a Bescom cable (The Times of India).
moved.so_what: If you live there, keep a charged power bank and log each outage with Bescom so there is a record of the complaint.

moved.what: BMTC is raising accident insurance cover for its employees from ₹50 lakh to ₹1 crore (Deccan Herald).
moved.so_what: This covers staff, not passengers; do not assume a bus ticket brings the same cover, and keep your own accident insurance current.

moved.what: Unhygienically prepared halwa and date products were seized in Bengaluru (The Times of India).
moved.so_what: With the festival sweets season on, buy packed sweets from outlets that show a licence number and a date.

carry_over.prompt: A neighbour shows you steady monthly payouts from a land-backed scheme paying more than any bank: what is the tell?
carry_over.answer: A return that is higher than the market and also guaranteed, paid out to you by recruiting more people like you.
